title: IN-Flow: Instance Normalization Flow for Non-stationary Time Series Forecasting

problem.claim: Distribution shift caused by non-stationarity hinders time series forecasting performance.

gap.claim: Existing approaches either depend on specified statistics that may not capture unknown shifts or use architecture-specific mechanisms with limited compatibility across forecasting models.

contributions.claim: A decoupled forecasting formulation separates shift removal from forecasting without relying on fixed statistics or restricting forecasting architectures.
The formulation is formalized as a bi-level optimization problem that jointly learns the transformation and forecasting components.
IN-Flow is an invertible time series transformation network that stacks normalization layers with flow-based invertible networks.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe IN-Flow as a novel invertible network for time series transformation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data.
The authors report that the experiments demonstrate the superiority of their method.

narrative_sequence.summary: Non-stationarity creates distribution shifts that hinder forecasting.
Existing statistical and architecture-specific solutions do not adequately handle unknown shifts or broad model compatibility.
The proposed approach decouples shift removal from forecasting and models their joint learning with bi-level optimization.
IN-Flow provides the required expressive and bidirectional transformation through normalization layers and invertible flow networks.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data are reported to demonstrate method superiority.

source_observation.claim: The method separates distribution-shift transformation from forecasting and learns both jointly.

interpretation.claim: Separating a changing-data transformation from the downstream predictor may improve compatibility across forecasting architectures.

application.claim: Consider modeling distribution correction as an independently parameterized transformation coupled to the predictor through joint optimization.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when this separation improves performance or whether the transformation generalizes across all forecasting settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, baselines, quantitative results, or experimental conditions.
The abstract does not describe the optimization procedure, computational cost, or failure cases.
